components.name: Xray-core
components.purpose: Elarni session metrics, dependency security updates, checked private-field access, context cleanup, static-analysis fixes, endpoint-free probe traces and joined XHTTP probe work, and Hysteria authentication context propagation; AmneziaWG 3.1 client engine, WireGuard DNS and peer validation, explicit TLS verification policy and null-certificate rejection, and exact provider balancer selectors; HTTP proxy TLS ALPN compatibility, synchronized XHTTP/mKCP receive shutdown and XHTTP upload byte accounting before buffer ownership transfer; optional logical asset reader and required physical socket binding for the Windows embedded runtime; optional TUN session admission limits for Windows; case-insensitive Windows process names and executable/folder paths for per-app routing; sandbox-compatible macOS socket ownership lookup, Darwin TUN reader cleanup and idle CPU backoff; Windows TCP full-tuple process attribution, joined TUN reader/session shutdown, UDP ownership and error cleanup, and complete Darwin datagram writes; TUIC v5 client integration with pinned sing-quic, required UDP socket ownership and TLS, strict lossless import/share/backup contracts and isolated interoperability/lifecycle traffic regressions; preserve queued responses on normal WebSocket stream completion while retaining abnormal-close errors; per-core DNS and outbound-manager context ownership for parallel embedded mobile probes; XHTTP XMUX steers new streams away from connections busy downloading, with a tagged loopback latency harness; gRPC copies received hunks into pooled buffers instead of pooling protobuf-owned slices, which ratcheted the heap goal during downloads; TUN admission evicts the longest-idle session when full and frees idle DNS flows after 5 s; XHTTP hedges a stalled HTTP/2 handshake after 1 s and closes its XMUX clients when the core stops; stable per-session Windows TUN adapter names, with the adapter parked between connects; QUIC path-MTU discovery on Android for Hysteria and XHTTP/3; gRPC and Hysteria close and forget their pooled clients when the core stops, so a stopped core's connections and the core itself no longer outlive it (Hysteria after XTLS/Xray-core#7107), with pool-release tests; a consumed session ActivityTimer drops its cancel callback, because the stopped runtime timers that still point to it kept the session context and the stopped core reachable for up to the idle timeout, and the gRPC dialer keeps copies of the session ID and outbounds instead of the first dial's context and connection, which gRPC's stopped idle timer kept for up to 30 min; loopback re-entry keeps its origin's SkipDNSResolve instead of forcing it, so the re-entered policy can resolve hostnames for IP rules; WireGuard retries a failed start instead of closing its TUN; XHTTP retires a shared connection only on transport failure or its own setup/response bound, not when a caller gives up, with a test-only setup-timeout override and the request-lifetime tests next to the transport; XHTTP packet-up dials the next XMUX connection's HTTP/2 handshake before moving its posts there and keeps posting on the old one meanwhile (at most 64 requests past its limit), so a request-limit rotation no longer holds uploads for a TCP and TLS handshake, with a loopback rotation test; XHTTP XMUX gives UDP flows other than QUIC their own connection within maxConnections (TCP streams keep the rest), because a download's 4 MB HTTP/2 window queued at the server in front of a call or game on a shared connection delayed it by seconds, with a loopback test on an emulated 20 Mbps, 50 ms line and the line emulator shared with the tagged latency harness; buffered writes flush and continue after a partial buffer write (upstream #6723), which failed Trojan connections whose first payload exceeded the buffer's free space; TUIC sends its CONNECT alone after 100 ms without a first payload, or once the client half-closes without one, so servers that speak first (SMTP, IMAP, MySQL) are reached; WireGuard reads each UDP reply whole instead of truncating it at 8 KiB; XHTTP posts and a session's current upload connection hold their XMUX connection open, so retiring an HTTP/3 connection no longer closes it under posts in flight; XHTTP post bodies can be read again, so HTTP/2 resends the posts a front server's graceful GOAWAY left unprocessed instead of ending the session; HTTP/1.1 packet-up pipelines posts on a pool that reuses its connections, counts a post as written once it is on a connection, reads every response in order so a rejected post fails the session, sends again only the posts a server provably did not read (after Connection: close or a clean close), and closes idle or retired upload connections, including one a post returns after its client closed, instead of leaving them to the garbage collector; XHTTP splitConn.Close reports the reader close error; an embedder can report through internet.SocketPathChanged that its required socket binding moved, and WireGuard then reopens its socket there; the log tap names the level it keeps, so messages neither it nor the handler wants are not built; the WireGuard netstack returns injected packet buffers to gVisor's pools, caches tunnel DNS answers for their TTL, caps TCP receive buffers at 2 MiB (a stalled reader held 4 MiB each), passes queued packets to wireguard-go in batches, and lowers a tunnel MTU above the standard engine's smaller message buffers; the WireGuard bind reads and writes datagram batches with recvmmsg/sendmmsg on Linux, while AmneziaWG keeps single-datagram batches; direct UDP flows on Unix wait for a datagram without a buffer and borrow a pooled 64 KiB one to read it whole (each waiting flow held 64 KiB); the HTTP, TLS, BitTorrent and uTP sniffers reject a short first payload from the bytes they have, so a connection that starts with a few non-matching bytes is routed at once instead of after the 200 ms sniffing deadline; a Hysteria stream past the server's stream limit waits for credit instead of failing, without holding the client lock; TUIC enlarges its UDP socket buffers, which quic-go cannot reach behind the ownership wrapper, and starts with a 16 MiB connection window so two stalled downloads no longer block new streams; XHTTP's HTTP/2 client advertises 2 MiB stream windows instead of Go's 4 MiB, which each stalled download kept full; on Windows the WireGuard netstack's gVisor reads time from the performance counter, because Go's monotonic clock there moves in system-timer steps, so gVisor measured short round trips as zero and its RACK loss detection resent segments in flight; TUN TCP buffers are capped at 1 MiB receive and 2 MiB send (a stalled app or upload held 8 and 6 MiB); the Linux TUN opens with a virtio_net_hdr and TCP segmentation offload so gVisor exchanges 64 KiB segments with the kernel; TUN TCP connections hand gVisor up to 64 KiB per write and, while the stack holds more, take up to eight buffers per read instead of one; the TUN stack starts its packet reader only after its handlers are set; Linux process lookup tries the recent socket owners before scanning every process; the WireGuard netstack caps TCP receive buffers at 1 MiB on iOS, whose packet tunnel is killed above about 50 MB (40 stalled downloads held 120 MB at 2 MiB; a stalled download holds about 1.1 times the cap); connections to ports where the server speaks first (FTP, SMTP, POP3, IMAP, submission, MySQL, VNC) skip the 200 ms sniffing wait and the outbounds' wait for a first payload (500 ms for VLESS and HTTP, 100 ms for Trojan, VMess, Shadowsocks and TUIC), since their client sends nothing until the greeting; the Hysteria client's QUIC configuration is built by newQuicConfig, with stalled-download tests for Hysteria2 and XHTTP/3 against the patched quic-go; Mux.Cool skips its 100 ms wait for a first payload on those server-first ports too; a TUIC stalled-download test against the patched sagernet quic-go; the WireGuard netstack takes TCP source ports in turn instead of at random, because a server's gVisor stack drops a SYN for a port it still holds in TIME_WAIT, which hung a busy tunnel's connections for up to 60 s; the WireGuard bind asks for 7 MiB UDP socket buffers as wireguard-go's own bind does (forced on Linux when permitted), because the defaults overflowed under several streams and 8 downloads at 40 ms RTT ran slower than one; TUN UDP flows hand their whole backlog to the outbound in one read, and uTLS and REALITY client connections pack small buffers into full ones before writing; a ShadowQUIC outbound (proxy/shadowquic, infra/conf/shadowquic.go) that runs the Rust ShadowQUIC client in-process or as a program next to the core; AmneziaWG sends Jmax equal to Jmin when a profile names only Jmin, as amneziawg-go v3.1.20261116 refuses Jmin above a missing (0) Jmax, and a test that the "firefox" fingerprint completes a handshake with a server that picks P-256; WireGuard and AmneziaWG renew their keys with a handshake when the wall clock shows the device slept 60 s or more within 180 s of monotonic time (proxy/wireguard/sleep.go), because both engines age keys by Go's monotonic clock, which stops during sleep, and kept sending with a key the server had dropped for 15 s of awake time; the DNS outbound's UDP answers keep the address records that fit 512 bytes, or the query's EDNS size within 512..1,232, instead of up to 8 KiB the asker dropped; an IPv6-only lookup ends at the first resolver that answers without records instead of waiting for the next one; Hysteria2, TUIC and XHTTP/3 try up to four addresses of a server name in turn within their existing dial budget (as many as get at least 3 s each, each attempt getting the time left over the addresses left, IPv4 and IPv6 alternating from the address the dial picked before), start with the address that answered last and forget it on a socket path change, keep the one destination under a final mask other than salamander and udphop (FinalMask.UDPMasks), and stop at a Hysteria2 password refusal with its own error, with loopback tests against a silent [::1] address; the DNS outbound's checkIPv6 option (proxy/dns/ipv6_check.go): it finds out with a TLS hello to two public services whether the route of the asking inbound reaches public IPv6, and leaves public addresses out of AAAA answers while only IPv4 answers, so apps stop sending IPv6 to a server that has none; the Windows TUN's IPv4 routes go through another address of the adapter's own subnet (proxy/tun/route_next_hop.go) instead of on-link, because mirrored WSL copies on-link routes to Linux as scope link and Docker found no free subnet under them; on-link stay IPv6, routes wholly in multicast or to the limited broadcast, and routes inside the adapter's subnets, and the adapter's addresses are set before its routes are added; XDNS TCP resolver's Close closes its workers' connections and waits for the workers, and a worker gives up an answer after 5 s; the XDNS DNS-over-HTTP/3 resolver closes its packet conn before the QUIC transport, and both when the QUIC dial fails; the TUN reader ends on EBADF, EBADFD, ENXIO and ENODEV and warns of a repeating read error once a minute with a count; RandBetween draws a range narrower than 2^63 from crypto/rand without big.Int; REALITY sends the randomizednoalpn hello without ALPN, logs the swap of a randomized fingerprint once, and makes its auth key with the X25519 key that the server reads

components.name: libXray
components.purpose: Elarni FFI integration, bounded runtime metrics and ping controls, dependency security updates, parallel JSON probes with serialized startup/asset loading and joined cleanup quarantine, sanitized stage/status results, disposable DNS controls, exact HTTP response contracts, active packet-path probes, registered probe cancellation, enclosing deadlines, and distinct packet-path DNS failures; strict complete client profile import, 3x-ui protocol and transport preservation, WireGuard/AmneziaWG exports, compatible Clash graphs, and Telegram handoff validation; core DNS bootstrap host matching, TLS/REALITY/ECH/encryption and paired protocol traffic checks, and full-profile FFI routing checks; Windows helper, encrypted catalog, bounded subscriptions and QR import, transactional geodata revisions and independent elevated TUN validation; authenticated Windows listeners, opt-in runtime metrics streaming, bounded memory/session controls and dynamic WFP route enforcement; Incy input normalization using the official crypt1 codec, provider sharing restrictions and local QR encoding; shared pinned subscription downloads, ordered fallback approvals, domain migration, provider banners, verified TLS fronting/ClientHello fragmentation and cancellable desktop fetch operations; password-encrypted portable catalog backups with shared validation; release in-memory geodata after reusable Windows VPN shutdown; TUIC v5 client integration with pinned sing-quic, required UDP socket ownership and TLS, strict lossless import/share/backup contracts and isolated interoperability/lifecycle traffic regressions; stable per-session Windows TUN adapter names; Windows helper install hashes while copying, pre-launches the installed copy and runs from the MSI; the Windows catalog lease process serves loadCatalog/saveCatalog for its owner; a core stop/start regression for gRPC, Hysteria and XHTTP that checks sockets and goroutines return to baseline and the stopped cores become unreachable, and the unelevated staleVPNGuard check that lets Windows connects and app start clear a crashed helper's DNS guard; Windows TUN MTU 9000; the Clash alias walk charges queued nodes against its expansion budget, so self-referencing anchors cannot exhaust memory; the subscription User-Agent carries the app version, which the elarni-core fetch test checks against pubspec.yaml; compiled-routing tests that load the Rust compiler's output into Xray's router, including loopback re-entry; elarni-core --uninstall-helper, which the MSI runs on uninstall to stop running helper copies, clear a stale DNS guard and delete the helper folder; CI names the pinned wintun.dll so its load test cannot skip; the Windows benchmark binding reads the socket family before bind and rejects unknown interface indexes; the TUN DNS outbound forwards query types other than A/AAAA (HTTPS/SVCB excepted) to the profile's first IP resolver through the profile's DNS route instead of answering them empty; the Windows physical binding reports a default route that moved to another interface, so WireGuard leaves the old adapter; Windows TUN routes keep each included prefix instead of merging it into a covering route, so a host listed beside a default still outranks a longer physical route; Clash Hysteria2 up/down and hop-interval follow Mihomo (a bare number is Mbps, B is bytes, decimal prefixes, unparsed rates ignored, N-M hop ranges with a 5 s floor); v2rayN VMess QR codes keep the gRPC authority from host and the insecure, vcn and pcs certificate policy; WireGuard links and configs accept v2rayN's reserved bytes (1,2,3); Clash ws-opts read the Host header in any case, so it becomes the TLS SNI as in Mihomo; base64 feeds whose text starts with a BOM, or that are unpadded and wrapped into lines, import; the app log tap tells the core its level, and geodata reduction decodes one entry at a time instead of the whole list; macOS and Windows run the core on two Ps unless GOMAXPROCS is set, which cut CPU per GB for WireGuard and Hysteria2 on macOS by more than half and halved it in Windows VPN mode; runtime metrics read the heap from runtime/metrics instead of stopping the world, and the desktop VPN relays send a metrics frame only when traffic, sessions or logs changed, or every 10 s; ShadowQUIC links, Clash proxies and sharing, and the pinned ShadowQUIC client program in the elevated Windows and Linux helpers; the compiled-routing test checks that the Mac and iPhone tunnel's own subnets are blocked except for DNS

components.name: tun2proxy
components.purpose: joined session shutdown, preservation of fragmented DNS-over-TCP responses, and unconnected SOCKS UDP relay sockets compatible with Darwin send_to, and TCP_NODELAY on the proxy connection; session limits and counters per protocol with sessions reserved for DNS, DNS sessions that end with their answer, and DNS answers forwarded as received; bytes read with the last SOCKS reply delivered to the client, and ICMP echo requests answered; only the library the Apple packet bridge runs is kept (SOCKS5 sessions and DNS over TCP): the command-line programs, the HTTP and SOCKS4 proxies, virtual DNS, the UDP gateway, socket transfer between namespaces, the Android and Windows service entry points, the C API and the build script are removed

components.name: quic-go
components.purpose: received stream bytes count as read for the connection window up to twice its maximum, so downloads the application stopped reading no longer freeze every stream of a Hysteria2 or XHTTP/3 connection; go.mod tidied for the copied non-test sources; http3 imports sorted by gofmt; a send failing with ENOBUFS (SagerNet/quic-go e86a8a79) or, once the handshake is complete and for up to 5 s of failed sends, with a lost interface, route or local address drops that packet instead of closing the connection; upstream quic-go fixes for a send stream reset during a blocked Write that never completed (254a5393), the crypto stream limit applied to out-of-order data instead of the offset (#6265) and packets from a discarded ACK range taken as new (#6308); upstream quic-go fixes for sending that stopped when the send queue freed up before the run loop checked it (#6223), DATAGRAM frames packed ahead of control frames and retransmissions (#5970, the order only, with a DATAGRAM frame that waited ten packets sent first instead of dropped) and a handshake that timed out on an interface refusing the initial packet size, which now falls back to 1200 bytes (#5911, ported to v0.61), with a congestion controller installed by the application told every size above its seed and never a smaller one, the cubic sender taking only that decrease, the refused packet kept off the amplification limit, direct writes only until the initial size was tried, and the default size still read from Config

components.name: sagernet-quic-go
components.purpose: received stream bytes count as read for the connection window up to twice its maximum, so downloads the application stopped reading no longer freeze every stream of a TUIC connection; go.mod tidied for the copied non-test sources; a send failing with a lost interface, route or local address once the handshake is complete drops that packet instead of closing the connection for up to 5 s of failed sends, as ENOBUFS already did; upstream quic-go fixes for a send stream reset during a blocked Write that never completed (254a5393), the crypto stream limit applied to out-of-order data instead of the offset (#6265) and packets from a discarded ACK range taken as new (#6308); the Vendor/quic-go ports of upstream quic-go #6223, #5970 and #5911 (send queue stall, DATAGRAM frame order with a DATAGRAM frame that waited ten packets sent first instead of dropped, fallback to 1200 bytes with its congestion-controller seed, amplification and Config fixes); SagerNet/quic-go mod.7, mod.12 and mod.13 (0cae1a77, 80c132fe, 2e73222e) as upstream ships them, which rework how application-limited periods reach the congestion controller (TUIC with BBR) and stop ACK-only packets from using the cubic pacer's budget

components.name: wireguard-go
components.purpose: message buffers sized for one packet (2016 bytes) instead of 64 KiB on desktop and Android, since Xray's bind and gVisor TUN use no UDP GSO/GRO or TUN offload; a test reads its atomic counter for go vet; upstream fixes for an IPv6 length that overflowed uint16 on receive (b3bc704ef0) and a handshake response consumed after an intermediate initiation (2631ce99a0)

components.name: shadowquic
components.purpose: ShadowQUIC v0.4.12 client fixes and memory reductions listed in Vendor/shadowquic/ELARNI_PATCHES.md (bounded message decoding, UDP relay robustness and send path, pooled unidirectional streams, 0-RTT handling, SOCKS5 fixes, endpoint and resolver fixes, smaller buffers); the SOCKS listener reports its bound address; the global allocator is a feature that Elarni leaves off; only the library is kept: the command-line program, the REST interface's dependencies, the build script, the integration tests and the packaging files are removed
